```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

This article demonstrates how to work with time-varying covariates, compare
screening approaches, and launch the interactive diagnostics app.

```{r}
library(PharmaStatsR)
set.seed(123)
data(pharmo_example)
```

## Compare Screening Methods

These screening methods fit ordinary regression models, which do not model
within-subject correlation. LASSO can hold out entire subjects during
cross-validation using `id`. The BIC approach compares candidates separately;
it is not a joint Bayesian model. Use these outputs as exploratory candidates
for a reviewed model specification.

```{r}
covs <- c("WT", "AGE", "CRCL")
sel_step <- screen_covariates_stepwise(pharmo_example, "DV", "SubjectID", covs)
sel_lasso <- screen_covariates_lasso(
  pharmo_example, "DV", covs,
  id = "SubjectID", nfolds = 5
)
sel_bayes <- screen_covariates_bayesian(pharmo_example, "DV", covs, min_bf = 3)

list(stepwise = sel_step, lasso = sel_lasso, bayesian = sel_bayes)
```

### AIC/BIC input requirements

Stepwise and BIC screening accept a real numeric response and numeric, logical,
character, or factor candidates. They filter rows once using the response and
**all** candidates, so every model comparison uses the same observations.
Missing values in unrelated columns, including the stepwise subject identifier,
do not remove rows. Numeric values must be finite on the retained rows.

At least three rows must remain, and both the response and each candidate must
vary on those rows. A factor can become constant after filtering even when it
varies in the original table. Such inputs now raise an error with the affected
column name. Review or remove unsuitable candidates explicitly before retrying.
Unused factor levels are dropped, and character candidates are treated as
factors. These minimum checks do not resolve collinearity or guarantee that a
large model can be estimated from a small sample.

Column names are literal names, not formula expressions. For example, a column
called `dose + weight` is one candidate, and a selected categorical column is
returned as a whole term rather than individual contrast coefficients:

```{r}
set.seed(42)
literal_names <- data.frame(
  SubjectID = seq_len(100),
  "dose + weight" = rnorm(100),
  "treatment group" = factor(rep(c("A", "B"), 50)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
literal_names[["drug response"]] <-
  5 * literal_names[["dose + weight"]] +
  3 * (literal_names[["treatment group"]] == "B") + rnorm(100)

screen_covariates_stepwise(
  literal_names, "drug response", "SubjectID",
  c("dose + weight", "treatment group")
)
screen_covariates_bayesian(
  literal_names, "drug response", c("dose + weight", "treatment group")
)
```

Column and candidate names must be unique; the response cannot also be a
candidate. An empty candidate selection returns `character(0)` without fitting.
The BIC `min_bf` threshold must always be a finite positive numeric scalar,
including when the candidate selection is empty. An empty result after screening
means that no candidate met the selection criterion; unusable data raises an
error instead. Literal-name support described here applies to these two
screening functions. Mixed-model fitting can opt into literal names with
`repair_names = TRUE`; its strict default still requires syntactic names.

## Reuse a subject-level split

Generate fold labels once at the subject level and map them to the original
rows. The same split can then be reused when comparing LASSO and elastic net.
`foldid` takes precedence over `nfolds`; supplying `id` as well rejects any
assignment that splits a retained subject across folds.

```{r}
subjects <- unique(pharmo_example$SubjectID)
set.seed(123)
subject_folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = length(subjects)))
folds <- subject_folds[match(pharmo_example$SubjectID, subjects)]

lasso <- screen_covariates_lasso(
  pharmo_example, "DV", covs,
  id = "SubjectID", foldid = folds
)
elastic_net <- screen_covariates_lasso(
  pharmo_example, "DV", covs,
  alpha = 0.5,
  id = "SubjectID", foldid = folds
)
list(lasso = lasso, elastic_net = elastic_net)
```

Keep one fold label for every original row, including rows with missing
responses or candidates. The wrapper removes incomplete rows and their fold
labels together, then renumbers the surviving labels. At least three folds
must remain. When generating random folds, choose `nfolds` no larger than the
number of retained subjects (or rows when `id` is omitted).

The split balances subject counts, not observation counts. Cross-validation
still uses the backend's observation-weighted error, so subjects with more
records have more weight. Grouping does not refit preprocessing: imputation or
feature transformations supplied before this call are shared across folds.
For model evaluation, fit preprocessing on each training fold separately in
an evaluation workflow. See the [glmnet reference](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/glmnet/html/cv.glmnet.html)
for details of the underlying cross-validation calculation.

For numeric mean/median or nearest-neighbor imputation inside training folds,
use the separate
`screen_covariates_lasso_imputed()` helper with a prespecified `lambda` grid.
It retains rows with missing predictors and returns held-out predictions,
fold replacement tables or donor models, and the final model; see the data-preparation vignette
for a worked example. Set `encode = TRUE` to fit additive categorical encoding
inside each training fold as well; missing or unseen categorical values fail.
Selection maps nonzero design columns back to raw variables, without a grouped
penalty or post-selection inference. Use `predict_lasso_imputed()` to apply the final saved
imputer and restore predictor order when predicting new rows. Categorical
preprocessing within folds remains manual.

## Validate a mixed-effects fit

`fit_covariate_model()` fits additive fixed effects and a random subject
intercept using the default REML method in `nlme`. Its response must be numeric;
the subject identifier and covariates can be numeric, logical, character, or
factor vectors. Response, identifier, and covariate roles must be distinct.
An empty covariate selection fits an intercept-only fixed-effects model.

Rows missing any required value are excluded with `na.exclude`. On the retained
rows, numeric values must be finite and the response must vary. At least three
rows and two subjects must remain, with repeated observations for at least one
subject. The fixed-effects design must have full column rank and more rows than
coefficients. Constant or redundant predictors, or categorical predictors that
lose all variation after exclusion, need to be reviewed before fitting.
These checks do not guarantee convergence or establish scientific adequacy.

The backend requires syntactic names internally. Set `repair_names = TRUE` to
record collision-free aliases while keeping original names in your input data:

```{r}
model_data <- pharmo_example
names(model_data)[names(model_data) == "WT"] <- "body mass"
model <- fit_covariate_model(
  model_data, "DV", "SubjectID", c("Time", "body mass", "AGE"),
  repair_names = TRUE
)
model$column_map
nlme::fixef(model)
head(predict_covariate_model(model, model_data))
head(predict_covariate_model(model, model_data, level = 1))
```

The result stays a native `lme` object. Its formulas, coefficient labels, and
stored data use the mapped backend names. Native `predict()` expects those
names; `predict_covariate_model()` instead selects original columns and applies
the saved map, including after RDS restoration. The caller's data are unchanged.
Strict calls without name repair retain their existing interface and data names.

The helper defaults to population predictions (`level = 0`), requiring only
covariates. `level = 1` requires the subject ID and adds its fitted intercept;
unknown subjects return `NA`, without a population fallback. Missing predictors
or required IDs raise errors. Results are numeric vectors named by input rows,
with singleton and empty batches supported. No intervals are added.

A fixed balanced reference in the tests has intercept `2`, slope `1.5`, four
subject offsets `(-3, -1, 1, 3)`, visits `(-1, 0, 1)`, and residuals `(1, -2, 1)`
within each subject. REML gives residual variance `24/7`, random-intercept
variance `116/21`, and subject-effect shrinkage `29/35`. These references verify
that repair and prediction preserve the numerical model.

## Reshape Time-Varying Covariates

```{r}
long_data <- pharmo_example[, c("SubjectID", "Time", "WT")]
wide <- reshape_timevarying(long_data, covariates = "WT")
back_long <- reshape_timevarying(wide, covariates = "WT")
head(back_long)
```

The function detects long format when the time column and every selected
covariate are present. Otherwise, it reads wide columns named
`<covariate>_<time label>`. Covariate names are literal, and the complete suffix
is kept as the time label:

```{r}
visits <- data.frame(
  SubjectID = c(1L, 1L),
  Time = c("pre_dose", "post_dose"),
  dose_rate = c(2, 3),
  "WT(kg)" = c(70, 71),
  check.names = FALSE
)
visit_wide <- reshape_timevarying(visits, c("dose_rate", "WT(kg)"))
visit_wide
reshape_timevarying(visit_wide, c("dose_rate", "WT(kg)"))
```

Names containing spaces or punctuation also work for `id` and `time_var`.
Selections must be nonempty and unique, and every selected covariate must be
represented. Identifier, time, and covariate names must differ. If the time
column exists but some selected covariates are absent, the input is rejected
instead of guessing its format.

Each wide column must match exactly one selected covariate prefix. For example,
`x_y_0` is ambiguous when selecting both `x` and `x_y`: it could mean `x` at
`y_0` or `x_y` at `0`. Rename the covariates or reshape them separately in that
case. Empty time suffixes and output-name collisions also raise errors.

All columns other than time and the selected covariates identify wide rows.
Duplicate combinations of these identifying columns and time raise an error;
the helper does not aggregate repeated measurements. Metadata may distinguish
multiple rows for one subject. Retained metadata names must not start with a
selected covariate plus `_`, because those names would be read as repeated
measurements on the return trip. The explicitly selected `id` is exempt and
is always retained.

The pivot keeps explicit missing values and fills missing covariate/time
combinations with missing values. Consequently, sparse input can gain rows or
cells on a round trip. Long input requires at least one nonmissing, nonempty
time value; a wide table with zero rows can still supply its mapping through
column names.

Numeric-looking time labels are converted to numbers only when this keeps
distinct labels distinct and does not create missing values. Labels such as
`01` and `1` remain character when both occur, and literal `NA` and `NaN` labels
remain text. Original factor, date, and other time classes are not stored in
wide column names; restore the intended time class explicitly when needed.

## Weight-Allometric Nonlinear Fitting

`fit_nlmixr_allometric()` fits a prespecified one-compartment oral model with
first-order absorption. Subject-constant weight scales clearance with exponent
0.75 and volume with exponent 1; the exponents are fixed assumptions. Independent
normal subject effects act on log absorption and log clearance, with additive
normal residual error. Optional `nlmixr2est` is required.

```{r allometric-fit, eval=FALSE}
# Requires nlmixr2data too; a full stochastic SAEM fit can take several minutes.
fit_pk <- fit_nlmixr_allometric(nlmixr2data::theo_sd, weight = "WT",
  reference_weight = 70, control = list(seed = 99),
  initial = list(ka = 1.5, cl = 3.2, v = 32,
    eta_ka_var = 0.25, eta_cl_var = 0.36, residual_sd = 0.7)
)
attr(fit_pk, "allometry")$initial
head(fit_pk$PRED)
```

`initial` accepts positive finite natural-scale absorption, reference clearance
and reference volume. `eta_ka_var` and `eta_cl_var` are log-scale subject-effect
variances, while `residual_sd` is an additive response standard deviation.
Unspecified entries keep their original defaults. The stored `initial` vector
records all resolved starts, not fitted estimates. All parameters remain free
for estimation. Compare prespecified starts and seeds to examine sensitivity;
this interface does not search for or certify a global optimum.

The input must include explicit oral dose and observation records (`EVID`,
`AMT`), positive integer IDs, nonnegative time, and finite weight on every row.
Missing observation responses and time-varying weight are rejected. Infusion,
additional-dose, steady-state, censoring, and multiple-endpoint modifier
columns are unsupported even when zero. Weight and its reference must use the
same units; dose, volume, response, clearance and time units must be consistent.
The native fit can reorder rows and omit doses. Inspect convergence and model
adequacy separately. `fit_nlmixr_model()` remains the original fixed example.

See `help("fit_nlmixr_allometric")` for the complete event contract and metadata.
The [documentation site](https://diogoribeiro7.github.io/PharmaStatsR/) includes
workflow guides and the evidence inventory; the weight-allometric guide adds
the equations and numerical references when this version is published.

## Interactive Diagnostics App

```{r eval=FALSE}
model <- fit_covariate_model(pharmo_example, "DV", "SubjectID", c("WT", "AGE"))
run_diagnostics_app(model, pharmo_example)
```

Launch `run_diagnostics_app()` without arguments to upload a CSV. Required
columns are `SubjectID`, `Time`, and `DV`; additional covariates are optional.
Column names must be unique, and the uploaded names are preserved. Time and DV
must be numeric with no infinite values. Rows missing SubjectID, Time, or DV
are excluded from the built-in fit and prediction plots, while the original
loaded data are retained. Missing unused covariates do not exclude a row.
Preloaded data receive the same structural validation before the app launches.

Click **Fit model** to fit DV by Time with a random intercept for each subject.
This button uses that fixed specification even when other covariates are
present. To inspect a different fitted model, supply it with its corresponding
data when launching the app, as in the example above.

Upload and fitting errors appear in the status panel with the reason for the
failure. Each new upload clears the previous model. If the upload fails, the
previous data are also cleared, so old diagnostics cannot be mistaken for the
new file's results. A failed refit clears the old model while retaining the
loaded data. Upload corrected data and fit again to recover without restarting
the app.

The **Binned summary** tab shows observed percentiles and fitted medians. It
does not simulate predictive uncertainty. Choose a whole number of time bins
of at least two; changing the bins redraws the summary without refitting the
model. Invalid bin values show a message in that plot and leave the fit intact.
